I farm these 20 mu the same way most people here do, wheat first and then maize right after. I finished middle school, so I do listen to what the extension people say, but in the end I still go by what I saw on my own land and what the neighbors around me got last year. My land has well water, so I am not as scared of a dry spell as people without irrigation, but pumping costs money, and with some people in the house working off-farm, family labor is tight at busy times. So this year I will keep the wheat-maize rotation on all 20 mu, stay with varieties I know, and not make any big gamble.

For wheat, I will sow in early to mid October, not too early because warm autumn can make it grow too lush, and not too late because then it does not tiller well before winter. I will use a common improved wheat seed from the local dealer. Fertilizer, I will do about what worked for me before: some base fertilizer before sowing, then one topdressing around jointing. The extension man says not to overdo it, but if wheat looks pale in spring, I still prefer to add a bit rather than risk losing yield. I will probably irrigate three times if the weather is normal: once after sowing if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once around grain filling depending on rain. For maize, the key is speed. After wheat harvest in June, I want the maize in within a few days. There is no time for slow land preparation, so I will keep tillage simple and use the same 20 mu right away. I will use a hybrid maize seed because local hybrids give more stable yield. I will put most fertilizer near planting and then give one more round around the big bell stage if the crop looks worth it. If summer rain is decent, I may irrigate only once or even skip one turn, because pumping water for maize is expensive and sometimes the rain can carry it.
